title: Seat studs in a framing layout jig
instruction: Seat the four 2x4 studs on edge in the layout jig, tight against the end fence.
context: Before a pony wall or the framing under a window is nailed together, a framer lays the short studs into a layout jig: each stud stands on edge between a pair of stops at a fixed spacing and is pushed tight against the end fence, so the spacing and the ends come out right without measuring every piece. Done by: carpenters (framing).
setup: The two arm bases stand 61 cm apart on an oak table. A 3/4-inch (19 mm) plywood jig board, 106 cm wide and 48 cm deep, lies flat on the table, centred between the arms, its near edge 12 cm out from the arm bases. Across its far side stands an end fence: a 2x4 on edge (38 mm thick, 89 mm tall), as wide as the board, its face 56 cm out from the arm bases. Four slots run from the fence toward the arms, 12 inches (30.5 cm) on centre: their centre lines are 15.2 cm and 45.7 cm to each side of the midline between the arms. Each slot is a pair of wood cleats, 3/4 x 1-1/2 inch (19 mm wide, 38 mm tall) and 6 inches (152 mm) long, fixed to the plywood from the fence face toward the arms, 44.1 mm apart (a 38.1 mm stud has 3 mm to spare on each side). The top of each cleat is rounded over toward its slot with a 19 mm radius: its slot-side face is straight up for the lower 19 mm, then curves up and away to the full 38 mm at the cleat's outer edge. Four loose studs: surfaced spruce-pine-fir 2x4s, 38 x 89 mm, cut to 368 mm (14-1/2 inches), 0.56 kg each, all standing on edge (89 mm tall) with their length pointing away from the arms. Two stand on the plywood with their centres 36 cm out from the arm bases, 5 cm left and 5 cm right of the midline, turned 4.6 degrees counterclockwise (left one) and 3.4 degrees clockwise (right one), seen from above. Two stand on the table beside the jig with their centres 30 cm out, 58.5 cm left and 58.5 cm right of the midline, turned 5.7 degrees clockwise (left one) and 6.9 degrees counterclockwise (right one).
scoring: Each stud scores on its own, and each slot counts for at most one stud. A stud is seated in a slot if it stands on edge (its 89 mm face upright within 3 degrees), its length is square to the fence within 3 degrees, its bottom is within 3 mm of the plywood, its centre line where it passes the cleats is within 4 mm of the slot's centre line, at least 76 mm of its length (half the cleat length) is between the cleats, and it is still. A seated stud scores 0.15; a seated stud whose end is also within 2 mm of the fence face scores 0.25. The trial scores the sum, up to 1.0. It ends at 1.0 when all four studs are seated and within 2 mm of the fence and this holds for 1 s; otherwise it scores the sum at the last step. A stud lying flat, resting on the cleat tops, standing beside or behind a slot, tilted, turned, or on the table scores 0.
reset_notes: Stand the four studs back on edge at their starting places and angles. Nothing is consumed; the jig is fixed.
fidelity: Studs, plywood, cleats and fence are boxes at real size; studs weigh 0.56 kg (spruce-pine-fir). Each cleat's rounded top is 16 overlapping 19 mm spheres on a 19 mm box; they bulge about 19 mm past the cleat's outer side and leave 0.5 mm ridges. Friction is rubber-like (1.2 static, 1.0 dynamic), above wood on wood (about 0.4 to 0.5), so studs slide less than real lumber. Eased edges and grain are left out. Slots are 12 inches on centre, not 16, to fit the table. Nailing is not part of the task.
